lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand how food is moved through the gut by peristalsis

primer.text: You have seen the canal's regions and know food must travel through all of them without any skeleton to help. This lesson explains the muscle work that does it: rhythmic waves of contraction squeezing the bolus along, powered by two muscle layers and lubricated by mucus and fibre.

modules.title: Waves That Move the Bolus
modules.opening: Peristalsis moves food along the alimentary canal by waves of muscle contraction in its walls. Circular muscles squeeze the tube's diameter while longitudinal muscles shorten each section, pushing the bolus onwards; mucus keeps the passage slippery, and dietary fibre gives the muscles something firm to grip.
keyPoints: Peristalsis propels food through the alimentary canal by rhythmic contractions.
Circular muscles contracting narrow the lumen's diameter.
Longitudinal muscles contracting shorten the section involved.
Mucus lubricates the food mass and lowers friction.
Dietary fibre supplies the roughage the muscles push against.

low.restatement: Squeeze behind, shorten the wall, and the food advances.
low.analogy: Pushing toothpaste along the tube with your fingers.
low.examPointer: Name both muscle layers and what each contraction does to the tube.

medium.restatement: The two muscle layers act out of phase, so contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead create a travelling wave.
medium.analogy: A Mexican wave circling a stadium, each section acting in turn.
medium.examPointer: Attribute the wave to the gut wall's muscles, not to gravity.

glossary.definition: The rhythmic wave of muscle contraction that pushes food along the alimentary canal.
The rounded mass of food that peristalsis moves through the canal.
The hollow interior of the canal through which the food mass travels.
